input.title: The Signal Tower: Four Lights to Wake
input.designRationale: I am accountable for evidence quality first, polish second. The contract forbids feedback, hints, retries, and answer exposure during the four-item window, so the biggest design risk is that a nine-year-old experiences four silent questions as a test that ignores her — and disengages, giving us abandonment instead of evidence. My answer is a frame where silence is diegetic: she is the lone keeper of a dormant signal tower on a foggy coast, and each of the four lamps stores whatever she declares into it. Lamps store; they do not judge. The world reacts to COMMITMENT (a lamp charges and seals when she locks an answer, including 'not sure'), never to CORRECTNESS. This lets every response — correct, wrong, or uncertain — produce a satisfying, dignified world reaction without leaking evaluative information, which is exactly what the contract requires. The tower frame was chosen over a competitive or character-quiz frame because it needs no reading beyond the item sentences (the fog, lamps, and glow communicate state visually), it gives 'not sure' an honorable meaning ('leave this lamp on standby'), and it makes the no-retry rule legible ('a sealed lamp holds one message'). Her evidence (asked for harder riddles, questioned faulty logic) suggests she may tolerate the ITEM-4 trap of equal products; I treat that strictly as an engagement hypothesis and place ITEM-4 last per the contract sequence. Her documented hint-seeking is honored only after the window closes: a 'lantern of second looks' becomes available after all four lamps are resolved, and anything that happens there is reported separately. Every stimulus, factor pair, option set, credit rule, and confound flag is taken verbatim from the immutable contract; the frame adds presentation only.
independentlyChosenPrinciples: Silence must be diegetic: since no feedback is allowed, build a world where storing-without-judging is the natural behavior of the fiction, so the child does not read silence as coldness or as a hidden verdict.
React to commitment, not correctness: every lock-in (including 'not sure') produces the same magnitude of world response, so world reaction carries zero information about the answer.

'Not sure' must cost dignity nothing: it is framed as a deliberate keeper's decision ('standby'), visually equal in ceremony to a numeric answer, so stalling becomes recorded missing evidence instead of forced guessing — directly matching her documented tendency to stall and seek hints.

One screen, one stimulus, one sentence: reading is an excluded construct, so every item screen holds the contract's single sentence, the visual, and the response controls, nothing else; all frame narrative lives on the opening screen and is also conveyed pictorially.

Big targets, coarse motor: all interactive elements are at least 96px touch targets on the 1365×768 viewport; number entry is tap-a-tile from a 1–10 palette, never typing or dragging, because pointer precision is excluded from measurement.

Color aids parsing but never answers: group clusters may share a warm palette against a cool fog background to make 'bunch-ness' visible, but no color count, highlight, or animation ever encodes the correct quantity or option.

Confirmation before sealing: every response requires a second tap ('Send to the lamp'), separating exploration taps from committed evidence and protecting the latency keys from accidental-touch noise.

The instrument records its own failures: mis-taps, corrections before lock-in, screen-size issues, and long idle periods are logged as friction, so an ambiguous item can be downgraded rather than silently miscounted as a math error.
input.openingPromise: The opening screen shows a dark coastal tower with four unlit lamps and one line of large text with a matching picture: 'The tower sleeps. Four lamps wait for your messages. What you send is what they keep.' The promise is concrete and immediate: your answers are the fuel; four lamps, four messages, and the tower wakes when all four are resolved — lit or standby, the tower honors both.
input.firstThreeSeconds: Second 1: a dark tower silhouette with four visibly empty lamp sockets, gentle fog drifting — the emptiness itself states the goal. Second 2: the first lamp socket pulses softly and a single large 'Begin' button glows at center-bottom (≥120px, high contrast). Second 3: nothing else competes for attention; the only possible action is tapping Begin, so the child cannot be lost before the first item. No reading is required to know what to do; the pulse-plus-button is self-evident on touch or mouse.
input.firstAction: Tap the single glowing 'Begin' button. This transitions to ITEM-1's screen, where the first required evaluative action is equally unambiguous: the 4×6 dot-cluster stimulus appears with two clearly labeled answer slots ('bunches' and 'dots in each bunch', each label paired with a small icon: a circled-cluster icon for bunches, a single-dot icon for per-group) and a 1–10 tap-tile palette. The empty slot pulses to show where the first tap lands.
input.mission: Wake the sleeping signal tower by resolving all four of its lamps. Each lamp asks the keeper (the child) one question about what it sees out in the fog — bunches of dots, a rectangle of squares, a set of equal groups needing its matching equation, and two basket messages that may or may not say the same thing. The keeper sends one message per lamp. A lamp accepts a message and seals warm-lit; a lamp set to standby ('not sure') seals with a calm blue standby glow. When all four lamps are sealed either way, the tower wakes and sweeps its beam across the coast. The mission ends honorably whether lamps are lit or on standby, and the keeper may stop early — the tower simply holds the remaining lamps dark for another night, recorded as missing evidence.
input.coreInteraction: Per item: (1) the stimulus appears exactly as specified in the contract — the visual and its one sentence — centered and large; (2) the child inspects the countable shapes (dots, squares, or the two statements) at leisure, no timer; (3) she composes her response with taps: numeric fields are filled by tapping tiles from a 1–10 palette into labeled slots, the equation item is four large option cards plus a separate 'not sure' card, ITEM-4 is a two-part panel (same/different/not-sure cards, then a 1–10 palette for baskets in A); (4) a tapped value can be changed freely before commitment by tapping a different tile; (5) she commits by tapping 'Send to the lamp', which requires all fields of the item to hold either a value or 'not sure'; (6) the lamp draws the message up as light and seals. The loop is inspect → compose → revise-freely → commit → seal, four times.
input.mathAsPower: The mathematics IS the message. The only way to affect the world is to read multiplicative structure and declare it: naming the (groups, per-group) pair charges lamp 1; naming (rows, per-row) charges lamp 2; selecting the structurally matching equation charges lamp 3; discriminating whether swapped referents describe the same situation charges lamp 4. No decoration, exploration, or non-mathematical action moves the mission forward. Critically, the power granted is the power to COMMIT a reading of structure, not the power to be right — the lamp charge is identical for any committed answer — so mathematical thinking is the sole causal lever on the experience while the experience leaks nothing back about correctness. The causal chain a child perceives: 'I read the picture's structure → I send what I read → the lamp takes it and the tower gets closer to waking.'
input.responseAffordances: All responses are tap-based, no keyboard, no drag, no free text, honoring the contract's noFreeText and the excluded constructs. (a) Numeric entry (ITEM-1, ITEM-2, ITEM-4 second field): a horizontal palette of ten large tiles labeled 1–10; tapping a tile places it in the currently highlighted slot; tapping the other slot moves focus; tapping a new tile replaces the old value; slots are labeled with word + icon so vocabulary alone does not gate role assignment (contract confound). Reversed-role entries are accepted silently and recorded per the credit rules. (b) Single selection (ITEM-3, ITEM-4 first field): large option cards (≥96px height) in a fixed contract-specified set; ITEM-3 option order is randomized per session and logged, to control the position-bias confound named in the contract. (c) 'Not sure' is a visually equal card/tile on every field, styled as the standby lantern — never smaller, grayer, or shame-coded. (d) Commit: a single 'Send to the lamp' button, disabled until all fields hold something, with a brief press-and-hold-free two-state confirm (tap once to arm, tap again to send) so accidental touches do not commit. (e) A persistent 'Stop for tonight' door icon honors childMayStop at all times.
input.stakesAndConsequences: Stakes are structural, not evaluative: a sealed lamp holds exactly one message forever this night (retriesAllowed: 0), and the tower cannot wake until every lamp is resolved. This makes each commitment feel weighty — the arm-then-send confirm ritual embodies 'this one counts' — without ever threatening the child with being wrong, because the world never distinguishes right from wrong messages. Choosing standby has a real, visible consequence (that lamp glows blue instead of warm, and the final beam is narrower per standby lamp) but the tower still wakes and the ending is still honorable; the difference is descriptive ('two lamps lit, two on standby'), never a grade. Stopping early has the consequence the fiction predicts: the remaining lamps stay dark and the keeper's log truthfully says the night ended early. Nothing shames, nothing punishes, nothing loops her back; every path forward exists from every state.
input.recovery: Before commitment, everything is freely revisable: tapping a different tile replaces a value, tapping a different card changes a selection, and the arm state of the Send button can be canceled by tapping anywhere else. This means an accidental tap can never become recorded evidence. After commitment, the child is never trapped: the sealed lamp animation flows directly into the next item with no dead end, no error state, and no prompt to reconsider. If she commits 'not sure', the standby seal is as smooth as any other. If she goes idle for a long period, a gentle non-verbal pulse on the current slot reminds her where she is, and after extended idleness a soft prompt offers 'Standby this lamp?' and 'Stop for tonight?' as honorable exits — idleness converts to recorded missing evidence, never to a forced answer or a stuck screen. If she stops mid-item, the partial state is discarded and the item is recorded as omitted/abandoned, matching the contract's terminal outcome set. Instrument mis-fires (double-tap, mis-registered touch) are absorbed by the arm-then-send gate and logged as friction rather than answers.
input.progression: Progression is the tower itself: four lamp sockets are always visible in a slim, non-numeric status column at screen edge — dark (untouched), pulsing (current), warm-sealed (answered), blue-sealed (standby). The child can always see exactly how far she is and how much remains without any score, streak, or count of correct answers. Item order is fixed by the contract's prerequisite-first sequence (ITEM-1 → 2 → 3 → 4) and the visuals honor the reuse rules: dot clusters, square grid, equation cards, and the two basket statements are structurally and cosmetically distinct so no earlier screen previews a later item's structure — in particular, nothing before ITEM-4 ever shows a swapped-factor contrast. Perceived difficulty rises naturally (declare, declare, match, discriminate) which fits her documented appetite for harder problems late rather than early.
input.worldReaction: Correct, incorrect, uncertain, and recovered actions all produce the SAME class of reaction, differentiated only by commitment type, never by correctness. Compose taps: the tapped tile settles into its slot with a soft click and a faint ripple — acknowledgment that the input registered. Revision: the old value dissolves and the new one settles, communicating 'nothing is final yet'. Commit (any answer): the message lifts from the panel as a thread of light, the lamp drinks it, seals warm, and the fog near that lamp thins slightly — the world visibly moves regardless of what was sent. Commit ('not sure'): identical ceremony, blue standby seal, equal fog-thinning — uncertainty moves the world just as much. Stop early: the tower door closes gently and remaining lamps stay dark, a truthful, calm image. No reaction anywhere encodes the answer key: fog thinning, lamp brightness, and beam behavior depend only on how many lamps are resolved and by which commitment type the child can already see she chose — nothing she doesn't already know is revealed, and no pre-commitment cue (hover glow, option emphasis, palette highlight) ever differs across options.
input.payoff: When the fourth lamp seals, the tower wakes: the beam sweeps the coast once, fog rolls back, and small boats far out on the water light their own answering lanterns — the world acknowledges that the keeper did the night's work. The payoff scales with resolution, not correctness: each warm-lit lamp adds a beam ray and each standby lamp adds a soft blue harbor-light, so a four-standby night still produces a genuine, beautiful waking, just a quieter one — descriptively different, never judgmental. A keeper's log page then shows the factual record in child-readable pictures: four lamp icons in their sealed states and nothing about right or wrong. Only after this payoff — after all four responses are recorded and the evidence window is closed — does the 'lantern of second looks' appear as an optional door, honoring her documented liking for hints strictly post-window; anything behind it is logged as post-evaluation exposure, reported separately, and never alters the recorded evidence.
input.replayVariation: This evaluation is a single-administration evidence sample; the four exposure identities (EX-EQGROUPS-DOTS-4x6, EX-ARRAY-GRID-3x7, EX-EQUATION-MATCH-5x3, EX-REFERENT-SWAP-2x8) are single-use and must not recur, so 'replay' never means re-running these items. If she asks to play again, the tower frame supports future nights whose lamps carry the contract's evidenceRequiredNext probes (different factor pairs, different structures: a no-picture equal-group item, a column-reading array, an unknown-factor probe, the ITEM-4 disambiguation probe) authored as new exposure identities under the same rules — same world, fresh evidence, zero contamination. Cosmetic variation only (weather, time of night, boat positions) may change between nights; stimulus structure and factor pairs never repeat. Within this session there is no replay of any item: sealed is sealed.
input.visualDirection: Palette: deep blue-slate night sky and cool gray fog as the quiet ground; stimulus objects in high-contrast warm tones (amber dots, coral squares) so the countable things are the brightest elements on screen — honoring the small-sample preference for visible color while ensuring color aids parsing only (all dots identical amber, all squares identical coral; no color ever varies within or across groups in a way that could encode counts or the correct option). Composition: stimulus occupies the upper 60% of the 1365×768 frame at generous size — the 4×6 clusters with wide inter-cluster gaps so cluster count is legible at a glance; the 3×7 array with visible row seams and horizontal-row emphasis; ITEM-3's four equation cards in large friendly numerals; ITEM-4's two statements in short large-type lines with small basket-and-ball icons beside each statement to offload reading (highest-reading-load item per the contract's own confound note). Response controls occupy the lower band with ≥96px targets and ≥24px gaps. Typography: a round, highly legible children's sans at ≥28px for item sentences, larger for numerals. The tower status column is slim and desaturated so it never competes with the stimulus. Overall style: calm picture-book nightscape — warm where she must look, cool everywhere else.
input.motionDirection: Motion is slow, low-amplitude, and never on the stimulus during inspection: fog drifts at the periphery only; dots and squares are perfectly static so counting is never disturbed. Interactive motion is confined to acknowledgment: tile-settle (150ms ease-out), value-dissolve on revision (100ms), slot pulse at 0.5Hz on the awaiting field. The commit ceremony — light-thread rising to the lamp, seal, fog-thinning — runs ~2.5s and cannot be interrupted into a skipped record. Transitions between items are a 400ms crossfade with the tower column persisting for continuity. No motion ever differs by answer content: option cards share identical hover/press animations, and the palette tiles animate identically for every value. Idle pulse escalates gently (slightly larger pulse) rather than adding new elements. Nothing bounces, races, or times out.
input.soundDirection: A sparse, optional soundscape (visible mute toggle; all information also carried visually): low wind-and-water bed at very low volume; a soft wooden 'tock' for tile placement; a felt-mallet tone for arming Send; a rising two-note chime plus lamp-hum for sealing — the SAME chime for every commitment, warm and blue seals alike, so audio carries no correctness information; a single distant foghorn and layered lantern chimes for the tower-waking payoff, scaled by lamps-resolved count only. No error sounds exist because the world has no error states. No music with lyrics, no escalating tension audio, nothing that pressures pace on a no-time-limit instrument.
usefulLibraries: Pixi.js or plain Canvas 2D for the fog, lamp glow, and light-thread commit ceremony (GPU-friendly at 1365×768; keeps stimulus rendering crisp and static).
GSAP or Motion One for the small deterministic animation set (tile-settle, seal ceremony, crossfades) with precise durations that keep latency logging clean.
Howler.js for the optional sound layer with a global mute and preloaded short cues.

A tiny event-log utility (custom, or something like mitt + a ring-buffer logger) emitting timestamped structured events: first_entry, revision, arm, commit, not_sure, idle_prompt_shown, stop, mis-tap — feeding the contract's latency and friction keys exactly.

No physics, no UI framework requirement; if one is used, Preact/Svelte for the response panels only. Deliberately NO drag-and-drop or gesture libraries — the response contract forbids those interaction modes.
anticipatedChildConfusions: Role-slot confusion (ITEM-1/2): she may not be sure which slot means groups and which means per-group. Mitigation: word + icon labels on each slot (circled-cluster icon vs. single-item icon); the icons clarify what is being asked without hinting at the answer values. A genuine reversal is still fully recordable per the credit rules.

Total-reporting confusion (ITEM-1/2): she may compute 24 or 21 and look for one slot for it; the max tile is 10 so totals cannot be entered, but she may then place a total-adjacent guess. The two-slot layout plus icons signal 'two different counts'; if she still seems to seek a total, that behavior is itself contract-anticipated evidence (reported_total_instead_of_pair applies when entries reflect total-seeking).

Row vs. column reading (ITEM-2): 'rows' vocabulary may fail her even if structure-reading is intact. Mitigation: the row icon shows a highlighted horizontal band in a tiny generic 3-cell strip (structure of 'a row', never the 3×7 answer). A reversed reading remains cleanly recordable as c3_roles_reversed.

'Same' ambiguity (ITEM-4): she may read 'same' as 'same total' — the contract's named ambiguity. I cannot disambiguate in-window without teaching; the item ships as contracted, 'same' responses are auto-flagged c4_ambiguity_flag_requires_followup, and the frame makes the question situational ('do these two messages describe the same situation?') with distinct basket icons beside each statement to visually anchor 'situation'.

Sealing permanence: she may expect to fix a sealed lamp (children expect undo). Mitigation: the arm-then-send two-tap ritual plus a one-time pre-ITEM-1 pictorial notice ('a lamp keeps one message') sets the expectation before the first commitment; sealed lamps visibly lack any tap affordance.

'Not sure' misread as failure: she may avoid standby to avoid 'losing'. Mitigation: standby is styled as a dignified keeper's tool (a real lantern, equal size, calm blue) and the opening tower shows one distant already-standby harbor light as ambient normalization — no lamp of hers is pre-answered.

Silence misread as being wrong: with no feedback, she may interpret the neutral seal as disapproval. Mitigation: the seal ceremony is warm and identical for all answers, and the fiction ('lamps keep messages; the tower reads them at dawn') gives silence a sensible story.
instrumentRisks: Frame-induced caution: the weight of 'sealed forever' could push a careful child toward overusing 'not sure', inflating missing evidence. Monitored via not_sure_rate across items; if standby dominates all four, that pattern is reported as possible instrument-induced caution, not ability absence.

Ceremony latency contamination: the 2.5s seal ceremony and inspection-friendly pacing must not bleed into latency keys; time_to_first_entry and time_to_selection are measured from stimulus-fully-rendered to first meaningful input, excluding transitions, and this definition is logged with the data.

Icon leakage: slot icons and basket icons are designed to convey ROLE, never quantity; risk remains that an icon inadvertently cues an answer, so icons never depict the stimulus's actual counts (the row icon uses a generic 3-cell strip, cluster icons use an uncounted blob).

Touch-registration noise on a shared tablet could create phantom taps; the arm-then-send gate absorbs these, and any commit that follows an anomalously short compose phase is flagged for the friction log.
Randomized ITEM-3 option order controls position bias but must be logged per session or the c2 distractor keys lose interpretability.

Product-recognition shortcut on ITEM-3 (choosing by seeing 15) is a contract-named confound the instrument cannot remove; the guessing-control latency key and cross-item consistency checks carry that burden, and I must not present the groups in a way that makes 15 countable at a glance without structure (clusters spaced to invite group-wise reading).

Reading load on ITEM-4 is the highest in the set; the paired basket icons reduce it, but any sign of reading struggle (very long pre-response time with no interaction) is flagged so the construct can be downgraded to ambiguous per the confound gating.
input.engagementPrediction: Prediction: she completes all four lamps in one sitting of roughly 6–12 minutes, uses free revision at least once (consistent with her habit of questioning and checking logic), possibly slows markedly on ITEM-4 (the trap-like contrast should hold her attention given her taste for hard riddles), uses 'not sure' zero or one time, and asks to open the lantern of second looks afterward (consistent with her documented hint-seeking). I also predict she voices or shows interest in whether her sealed answers were right — an appetite the instrument deliberately does not feed in-window — and that the honest payoff plus post-window lantern is enough to keep the experience feeling fair rather than withholding. Continued-participation prediction: she would accept a 'second night' with new lamps (the evidenceRequiredNext probes) without resistance.
falsifyingEvidence: If she abandons before ITEM-3, my claim that diegetic silence sustains a no-feedback window for this child is falsified; the tower frame is insufficient and future nights need a stronger in-window (still non-evaluative) reason to continue.

If she taps 'not sure' on three or four items despite composing values first, the sealed-forever stakes likely induced caution — my stakes design is falsified as evidence-distorting and the permanence framing must be softened.

If time_to_first_entry on ITEM-1 exceeds a long idle threshold with no palette interaction, the finished screen did not make the first action understandable, falsifying my first-action design (icons and pulse were not enough).
If she attempts to tap sealed lamps repeatedly or shows distress at no-undo, my two-tap commit ritual failed to communicate permanence before the first commitment.

If ITEM-3 selection latency falls below the inspection threshold on a correct answer, the option-card presentation invited product-snap responding; my layout claim that spacing invites structural reading is weakened exactly as the contract's guessing control anticipates.
If she asks 'am I right?' repeatedly and stalls awaiting feedback, my prediction that the store-don't-judge fiction makes silence acceptable is falsified.

If friction logs show mis-taps or slot-focus errors on the 1–10 palette, my claim that the input mode keeps pointer precision out of the measurement is falsified and those items must be downgraded to ambiguous.
If she declines the post-window lantern entirely, my engagement inference from her hint-seeking history was an overreach — a useful correction to how much weight small-sample evidence deserves.
input.measurementResponsibilities: The instrument reports facts only, never mastery, proficiency, or preference. Per item it records: the committed response verbatim (both fields where applicable), outcome classification per the contract's credit rules including reversed-role, total-instead-of-pair, and distractor identities; 'not sure', omission, and abandonment as terminal outcomes classified as missing evidence, never failure; all contract measurement keys (c1_group_pair_correct, c1_roles_reversed, c1_reported_total_instead_of_pair, c1_not_sure_rate; c3_array_dimensions_correct, c3_roles_reversed, c3_reported_total_instead_of_dimensions, c3_off_by_one_count, c3_not_sure_rate; c2_equation_match_correct, distractor keys, c2_product_only_recognition_flag, c2_not_sure_rate, c2_selection_latency_below_inspection_threshold; c4_referent_discrimination_correct, c4_same_selected_product_equality_confusion, c4_referent_count_correct, c4_ambiguity_flag_requires_followup, c4_not_sure_rate); latency keys measured from stimulus-render-complete to first meaningful input with the definition logged; revision counts and pre-commit changes; friction events (mis-taps, idle prompts, focus errors); ITEM-3's randomized option order; assistance and exposure logs (which must be empty in-window — any nonzero in-window exposure is itself reported as an instrument violation); post-window lantern usage logged strictly separately. Output is the contract's per-construct evidence map — supported-provisionally, contradicted, ambiguous, or missing per C1–C4 — with all confound flags, applying the confound gating (sub-threshold-latency corrects downgraded to ambiguous; reading/input/pointer-interference flags downgrade the construct; every ITEM-4 'same' auto-flagged ambiguous pending the follow-up probe) and the cross-item consistency checks. Excluded from scoring, per contract: reading time, spelling, typing speed, keystroke counts, pointer path/precision. No outcome combination, including four correct, is ever reported as mastery; one item per construct is a single observation, and the report says so explicitly.
